# Really high idle after tightening spark plugs

Tightening a loose spark plug can introduce an immediate, dramatic change in engine behavior, but the mechanism behind that spike is often misunderstood as a simple "ECU learning" event. In your specific case involving the BMW 740 with the M62 V8, the symptoms describedâa struggle to start followed by revs shooting toward redline and settling at roughly 2000 RPM before droppingâpoint directly to an open-circuit failure that was suddenly repaired.

When a spark plug is loose or not seated correctly, the primary cylinder affected cannot sustain a proper combustion event. In many engine management systems, including those found in the M62 era, the ECU relies on feedback from ignition coils or specific cylinder firing patterns to calculate load and air-fuel mixtures. If one cylinder fails to fire reliably due to an arcing gap caused by a loose plug wire connection or poor terminal contact, the system interprets this as a misfire condition in that specific cylinder.

The "tick" you heard prior to tightening the plugs was likely mechanical vibration exacerbated by incomplete combustion cycles causing uneven pressure pulses, but the high idle is strictly an electronic response to maintaining stability under perceived low-load conditions.

### The Open Circuit Scenario

When you tightened the plugs and started the engine, you effectively restored continuity to a circuit that previously had high resistance or intermittent breaks. If the ECU detects that a cylinder has gone from "misfiring" (open circuit) to "firing normally" (closed circuit), it must instantly recalibrate its fueling strategy.

In many OBD-II systems, if a cylinder is detected as misfiring for more than one or two cycles, the ECU may enrich the air-fuel mixture globally or specifically for that bank to prevent stalling and reduce catalytic converter damage. However, some older engine control units employ a different logic: they assume that if a cylinder stops misfiring suddenly after a restart, the load on the engine has increased significantly because that cylinder is finally contributing torque. To compensate for this perceived sudden increase in mechanical load without triggering a limp mode or stalling, the ECU raises the idle speed target.

This explains why the revs shot up immediately upon restarting. The ECU thought, "We just regained power from Cylinder X. We need to boost the throttle opening and increase idle RPM to keep the engine stable while it figures out the new baseline." This is often referred to as an open-loop correction or a transient fuel cut-off override that results in high idle.

### Transient Behavior vs. Learned Values

Your observation that the car sat at 2000 RPM for 3â4 minutes before dropping to normal idle (around 900 RPM) is classic ECU adaptation behavior. The engine control unit does not instantly trust a sudden change in ignition performance. It enters a "limping" or cautious state, maintaining high idle speeds until it confirms that the new combustion pattern is stable over a sustained period.

During those first few minutes, the ECU was likely monitoring oxygen sensor data (O2 sensors) to verify that the air-fuel ratio remained within acceptable lambda limits despite the sudden reintroduction of the cylinder. Once the O2 sensors confirmed that the mixture was balanced and no further misfires were occurring, the adaptive fuel trims settled down, and the idle control valve commanded the throttle plate back to its standard closed-loop position.

Putting the car in gear forced the load up, which naturally dropped the RPMs regardless of the ECU's target, but returning to park removed that external load, causing the ECU to revert to its internal high-idle target until it could validate the new state again. After three or four restarts, the ECU had enough data points to confirm that the loose plug was no longer a fault condition, and the adaptive values stabilized permanently.

### Practical Takeaways for Engine Diagnostics

This scenario highlights why torque specifications are critical not just for preventing mechanical damage, but for ensuring electrical continuity. A loose spark plug can create an arc that mimics a misfire signal to the ECU, leading to strange idle behaviors once the connection is restored. If you encounter high idle after working on ignition components, do not assume the ECU has simply "learned" new tolerances in a neutral sense; it is actively compensating for a resolved fault condition.

For developers or engineers working with embedded systems, this mirrors handling a previously disabled input channel. When re-enabling a sensor or actuator that was disconnected, the system controller often defaults to a safe-high state until it validates the new input stream against historical baselines. Understanding this transient logic helps in troubleshooting why vehicles behave erratically immediately after repairs, even when the repair itself was mechanically successful.
